A revision you can defend

One artifact. One change. Your judgment.

Choose a slide, poster, or page you made. Work on a copy, remove personal information before sharing it with an AI tool, and follow your school’s AI-use rules.

  1. 1

    Make your own first attempt

    Name the audience, the main idea, and one thing that feels unclear. Make a revision before asking AI.

  2. 2

    Ask for a critique

    Prompt to adapt

    The audience is [audience], and the main idea is [idea]. Identify the single biggest obstacle to understanding it. Explain why. Do not redesign it for me.

  3. 3

    Choose one change

    Accept, adapt, or reject the critique with a reason. Keep the original beside your revision.

  4. 4

    Check what someone understands

    Show both versions to someone without explaining them. Ask what they understood first. Close the chat and explain your decision.

A starter exercise, not a measured learning intervention.

See a real revision and its limits

The Human Loop

Reach further while keeping the important thinking yours.

  1. Think & delegate

    Make a first attempt. Decide whether AI should give a hint, critique, comparison, or help you can check.

  2. Inspect & explain

    Question the assumptions and missing evidence. Explain the key idea with the chat closed.

  3. Verify & own

    Check a source, calculation, test, or actual behavior. Identify what you contributed.

Our developing framework. Start with hints when learning a skill; give an agent more responsibility when you can spot a failure.

Put it into practice

What does a new tool change?

One task. The same constraints. A result you inspect.

Choose a short task with a clear success condition. Give both tools the same task and constraints, then keep the outputs side by side.

Result
How well does the output meet your success condition?
Corrections
Which mistakes did you catch and fix?
Effort
What did it take to get something usable?

One comparison is a starting point, not a permanent ranking.
